title: Pretraining Objectives
oneLineScope: Causal LM, masked LM, next-sentence, span corruption — what the model is actually trained to predict.
prose:
Where we are. Two earlier threads meet at this node. From tokenization & subword units we have the atoms the model reads and writes — a finite vocabulary of subword pieces, and everything below operates on those, not on whole words. From scaled dot-product attention we have the machinery that lets every position mix information across a whole sequence in parallel. Put together, they give us a differentiable function that turns a sequence of tokens into a sequence of representations. But a function is not yet a model of anything: nothing so far says what it should learn. That is the gap this node closes — what the network is trained to predict, and where the right answers come from.

The gist. The defining trick of this era is self-supervision: take ordinary unlabeled text, withhold part of it, and train the model to predict the withheld part from what remains. Because the hidden part was already in the corpus, the corpus is its own answer key — unlabeled data becomes its own label, with no human annotation at all. The objectives in this node differ only in what they hide: causal language modeling hides the future and predicts the next token; masked language modeling hides scattered tokens and predicts them from both sides; next-sentence prediction asks whether two segments were adjacent; and span corruption hides contiguous runs and regenerates them.

Why it matters. This is the move that broke the data ceiling of the statistical-NLP era. When labels cost nothing, the training set can be the entire written web, and a model with hundreds of millions of parameters finally has enough signal to fit. The architecture lets you absorb that much data in parallel; self-supervision is what makes that much data available in the first place. Every later node about scaling presupposes this one: the reason there is anything to scale is sitting right here.

The idea: the text is its own label

Strip away the variants and one move remains. Take a passage of ordinary text, hide part of it, and train the model to predict the hidden part from the part you left visible. The thing predicted — a token, or a span of tokens — was already sitting in the corpus, so the supervision signal is manufactured for free from raw text. The field calls this self-supervised learning, to set it apart from supervised learning (a human provides each label) and from unsupervised learning in the older sense (density estimation with no prediction target at all). The name is a touch grandiose for what is, formally, just maximum likelihood on a cleverly chosen conditional distribution — a thing you know cold from n-gram language models and HMMs.

Make it concrete with the sentence “the cat sat on the warm mat.” Hide the last word and ask the model to predict “mat” from the rest; hide “sat” in the middle and ask it to recover that from both sides; or hide the run “on the warm” and ask it to regenerate the whole missing stretch. Each is a legitimate prediction problem with a known right answer, and each can be posed millions of times over from a single unlabeled corpus. That is the whole game; the rest of this node is just three disciplined ways of choosing what to hide.

What is genuinely new here is the scale it unlocks. Recall how sharply annotated resources bounded the statistical-NLP era: a treebank, a sense-tagged corpus, an aligned bitext each cost years of expert labor and capped out in the thousands or low millions of sentences. Self-supervision removes that ceiling at a stroke, because the labels are free — billions of tokens, no annotation budget. This is the single fact that made the whole era possible.

Causal (autoregressive) language modeling

Start with the oldest and simplest objective, the one behind the GPT lineage: predict each token from everything before it. Intuitively, the model reads left to right and, at every position, guesses what comes next — exactly what an n-gram model does, but with the entire history as context instead of a fixed window. Factor the probability of a token sequence \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\) by the chain rule, left to right:

\[ p_\theta(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = \prod_{t=1}^{n} p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{where \(\theta\) are the model parameters and \(x_{ \[ \mathcal{L} = -\sum_{t=1}^{n} \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{Read it as the familiar n-gram objective with one change: the conditioning context \(x_{entire preceding sequence fed through the network, not a fixed window of \(k\) previous words. The single architectural requirement is that position \(t\) must not see tokens at or beyond \(t\) when predicting \(x_t\) — otherwise the task is trivial and the model just copies the answer. That requirement is enforced by the causal mask from the scaled dot-product attention node: above-diagonal scores set to \(-\infty\) before the softmax, so each position attends only to its own past. This is why causal LM is the natural objective for a decoder-only model (the autoregressive LM node). And it is gloriously data-efficient: because the mask makes every position's loss depend only on legal context, a single forward pass over an \(n\)-token sequence yields \(n\) next-token predictions and \(n\) loss terms at once — every token is a training example. (Feeding the true history rather than the model's own guesses during training has a name you will meet again: teacher forcing.)

Masked language modeling

Predicting left to right has a cost: when the model builds a representation of token \(t\), it has only seen the left context. But for understanding a word in place — the antecedent of a pronoun, the sense of a homonym — the right context matters just as much. BERT's objective buys bidirectional context by changing what is hidden: instead of the future, corrupt a scattered ~15% of the tokens and predict those, using the full surrounding context on both sides. This is the old cloze task from psycholinguistics, which you may know by that name, scaled up. The loss runs only over the corrupted positions:

\[ \mathcal{L} = -\sum_{t \in M} \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{\setminus M}) \]

where \(M\) is the set of masked positions and \(x_{\setminus M}\) is the sequence with those positions replaced. Scoring only the masked positions — not the tokens handed to the model intact — is the point: the model is graded on what it had to reconstruct. Because no token needs to be hidden from any other, there is no causal mask: every position attends to every other, which is exactly what makes this an encoder-only, bidirectional model (the masked LM node). One wrinkle worth knowing: of the chosen 15%, BERT replaces 80% with a special [MASK] token, 10% with a random token, and leaves 10% unchanged. The reason is that [MASK] never appears at fine-tuning time, so training exclusively on it would create a train/test mismatch; the random and unchanged cases blur that gap. Note that this objective is markedly less data-efficient than causal LM: only the masked ~15% of positions contribute a loss term per sentence, not all \(n\), so BERT extracts less signal from each pass.

BERT also trained a second objective, next-sentence prediction (NSP): given two segments A and B, a binary classification of whether B genuinely followed A in the corpus or was a random other sentence, meant to teach inter-sentence coherence useful for tasks like question answering and natural-language inference. It is worth flagging honestly that this one did not hold up. The RoBERTa study re-ran the recipe without NSP and found it contributed little to nothing — simply training masked LM harder, on more data, longer, with bigger batches and a fresh mask each epoch, matched or beat the full BERT recipe. NSP is a clean cautionary tale about the difference between a plausible objective and a useful one, and exactly the sort of seam this tutorial would rather show you than paper over.

Span corruption and denoising

The encoder-only and decoder-only objectives sit at two extremes. T5 (the encoder–decoder contrast reframing) splits the difference with span corruption: mask out contiguous spans of tokens rather than scattered single ones, replace each dropped span with a single sentinel token, and train an encoder–decoder to emit the missing spans as a short target sequence. Concretely, the input “Thank you <X> me to your party <Y> week” pairs with the target “<X> for inviting <Y> last”. The encoder reads the corrupted text bidirectionally; the decoder generates the reconstruction autoregressively. So the loss is again next-token cross-entropy, but now over the target sequence of dropped spans rather than the whole input — which is precisely why this objective wants both halves of the architecture at once. BART makes the same denoising move with a menu of corruptions — token masking, deletion, sentence shuffling, span infilling — and trains the model to reconstruct the original document.

The T5 paper is especially valuable here because it ran the comparison systematically: it treats the objective as a knob — corruption rate, mean span length, and the choice among prefix-LM, scattered masking, and span corruption — and reports what each setting actually buys (their §3.1 and the experiments that follow), which is a far more honest way to learn this material than taking any single paper's choice as gospel. The headline finding is reassuring in its modesty: across that grid the denoising family is robustly strong, but no single objective dominates by a wide margin once data and compute are held fixed. The lesson is that the choice of what to hide matters less than the fact that you are hiding something at all and harvesting free labels by doing so.

The subtlety: objective and architecture are one decision

The point easiest to get backwards, and the one to carry forward, is that the objective and the masking are two views of a single choice. A left-to-right prediction target requires a causal mask and gives you a decoder-only generator (nodes on the autoregressive LM and decoder). A fill-in-the-blank target permits full bidirectional attention and gives you an encoder-only understander (the encoder / masked LM nodes). A span-reconstruction target wants an encoder to read and a decoder to write. You do not pick an architecture and then a loss; you pick what you want the model to predict, and that choice propagates back through the attention mask to the shape of the whole network. All three, note, predict the same kind of thing — the subword units from the tokenization & subword units node, not whole words — and all three bottom out in the same cross-entropy you already trust.

Where it leads

With the target settled, the open question is purely mechanical: how do you actually run the gradient descent — the optimizer, the learning-rate schedule, the batch sizes — that turns this loss into trained weights? That is exactly what optimization & training dynamics takes up next.

diagrams.caption: One sentence under three objectives: next-token (causal), masked-token (MLM), and span corruption (T5) — what each hides and what each predicts.
diagrams.altText: Three stacked rows, each showing the same example sentence 'the cat sat on the warm mat' tokenized into boxes. Row 1, labeled causal LM (GPT): all tokens up to a point are visible and an arrow predicts the single next token 'mat'; a note says each position predicts the next, left to right, behind a causal mask. Row 2, labeled masked LM (BERT): two scattered tokens 'sat' and 'warm' are replaced by [MASK] boxes and arrows point up from those positions to the predicted original words, using context on both sides; a note says predict only the masked positions, about 15 percent. Row 3, labeled span corruption (T5): a contiguous span 'on the warm' is replaced by a single sentinel box, and the target sequence to be generated is the dropped span; a note says reconstruct the missing span as a sequence.
diagrams.prompt: Structural diagram comparing three pretraining objectives applied to the SAME example sentence, drawn as three stacked horizontal rows, each row a sequence of small token boxes. Use the tokenized sentence: 'the' 'cat' 'sat' 'on' 'the' 'warm' 'mat'. ROW 1, labeled 'causal LM (GPT)': show the full sequence of token boxes; from the box 'warm' draw an upward arrow to a predicted box reading 'mat', emphasizing the predicted next token. Margin note with leader: 'each position predicts the NEXT token, left to right (causal mask: no peeking ahead)'. ROW 2, labeled 'masked LM (BERT)': show the same sequence but replace the boxes 'sat' and 'warm' with boxes reading '[MASK]'; draw an upward arrow from each [MASK] box to a predicted box showing the original word ('sat', 'warm'); show that context flows in from BOTH sides into each masked position. Margin note: 'predict ONLY the masked positions (~15%), using context on both sides'. ROW 3, labeled 'span corruption (T5)': show the sequence but replace the contiguous run 'on' 'the' 'warm' with a single box reading '<X>' (a sentinel); to the right, show a separate short target sequence the model must generate: '<X>' then 'on' 'the' 'warm'. Margin note: 'mask a contiguous SPAN; generate the missing span as a sequence'. Emphasize, in each row, which tokens are hidden and which are predicted. Label each row with its objective name. Structural diagram: the hidden and predicted tokens must be exact.

diagrams.caption: Self-supervision: the corpus manufactures its own labels, so training scales on raw unlabeled text.
diagrams.altText: On the left, a tall stack of plain text labeled 'raw text — no human labels'. A scissors-style 'hide part' step splits a sample sentence into a visible part and a hidden part. The visible part feeds into a box labeled 'model', and the hidden part becomes the training target, drawn as the label. An arrow from the model's prediction back to the hidden target is labeled 'cross-entropy loss'. A banner across the bottom reads: the data is its own label, so training scales on cheap unlabeled corpora with zero annotation.
diagrams.prompt: Conceptual diagram illustrating self-supervision as 'the data is its own label'. On the left, draw a tall stack of plain document pages labeled 'raw text — billions of tokens, NO human labels'. Pull one example sentence out of the stack. Apply a step labeled 'hide part of the text' that splits the sentence into two pieces: a 'visible part (input)' and a 'hidden part'. Draw the visible part flowing rightward into a box labeled 'model'. Draw the hidden part flowing into a slot labeled 'target / label — taken for free from the text itself'. From the model, draw a 'prediction' arrow meeting the target, with the meeting point labeled 'cross-entropy loss'. Across the bottom, a wide banner reading: 'the text supplies its own supervision → training scales on cheap unlabeled corpora, no annotation'. Emphasize the contrast with traditional supervised learning where a human must label every example. No equations and no tensor shapes; this is the intuition for WHY self-supervision unlocks scale. Conceptual analogy: meaning over precise labels.

bibliography.citation: Devlin, J., Chang, M.-W., Lee, K., & Toutanova, K. (2019). "BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding." NAACL.
bibliography.annotation: Primary source for the bidirectional, encoder-only objective. §3.1 specifies the 15% masking with its 80/10/10 mask/random/keep split and the next-sentence-prediction task — read it for the masking scheme and the train/inference mismatch that motivates the split.

bibliography.citation: Radford, A., Narasimhan, K., Salimans, T., & Sutskever, I. (2018). "Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training" (GPT-1).
bibliography.annotation: The autoregressive (causal) pretraining objective in the decoder-only setting; §3.1 gives the next-token log-likelihood used here. The origin of the GPT lineage's training target.

bibliography.citation: Raffel, C., et al. (2020). "Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer" (T5).
bibliography.annotation: Span corruption is in §3.1; the paper's lasting value is its systematic, controlled comparison of objectives (masked vs. autoregressive vs. denoising, span lengths, corruption rates) — read it to see the objective treated as a knob rather than a dogma. NSP's weakness is corroborated by Liu et al. (RoBERTa), arXiv:1907.11692.

bibliography.citation: Jurafsky, D., & Martin, J. H. "Speech and Language Processing" (SLP3 draft), chapters on language modeling and pretrained transformer models.
bibliography.annotation: The clearest textbook bridge from classical n-gram language modeling and the cloze task to causal and masked objectives, pitched for a reader with a statistics background. Best read for how the new objectives are continuous with the old ones.

expansion: Deeper treatment the prose deliberately omits, to be expanded strictly from the cited sources: (1) BERT's 80/10/10 masking rationale and the train/inference [MASK] mismatch in full (Devlin §3.1); (2) the RoBERTa ablation establishing that NSP is dispensable and that MLM benefits from more data, longer training, larger batches, and dynamic masking (Liu et al. 2019); (3) T5's controlled objective comparison — corruption rate, span length, and the i.i.d.-noise vs. span-corruption vs. prefix-LM settings (Raffel et al. §3.1 and the experiments that follow); (4) BART's specific corruption menu and why text infilling helped most (Lewis et al. 2019, arXiv:1910.13461); (5) the precise relationship between the autoregressive factorization and maximum-likelihood / perplexity, connecting to the classical n-gram framing. Cite each claim to its source section; do not introduce results from outside the bibliography.
